Neuromarketing report · RealEye webcam eye tracking

“Wake up the red in your hair”: two shampoo ad versions

What viewers noticed, in what order, and for how long, using RealEye's VAI, by gender, age and time window.

20 Nov 2026

How this was measured: This test was run on the RealEye platform with webcam eye tracking: viewers saw the images on their own devices and their gaze was recorded through their webcams.
FindingsWhat VAI meansViewing orderPer designComparisonGender and ageNext stepsTechnical appendix

Overall findings and conclusions

Conclusion: move the brand name into the warm zone and keep A's gaze cue, then test recall

In both designs viewers notice the tagline first, then the pack, the face, the logo and last the brand name banner, and that order does not change from the first 3 to the first 10 seconds. The brand banner is the weak spot: its VAI is 14.3 in design A and 8.3 in design B. Design A reaches the logo and banner more often; design B holds the face better. Without a recall result this is a diagnosis, not a winner.

All scores are RealEye VAI (0–100) and its three measures: Reach (how many viewers looked), Speed (how soon) and Hold (how long attention stayed).

Viewing order, both designsTagline → Pack → Face → Logo → Bannersame in the first 3, 5 and 10 s

Key findings

strength

Tagline and pack lead, in every window

Tagline VAI is 57.5 (A) and 57.6 (B) in the first 3 s with Reach near 80%. The pack follows (VAI 42.2 and 41.0) and catches up by 10 s (61.2 and 61.8). This part of the layout works.

risk

The brand name banner is the weak spot

Banner VAI is 3.6 → 7.5 → 14.3 in A and 1.2 → 3.6 → 8.3 in B (first 3, 5 and 10 s). Reach is 27% and 16% and Hold is about 1: few viewers get there, late, and only briefly. The heatmaps show the bottom band cold in every audience.

risk

Direct gaze helps the face and costs the brand

In B the face scores higher (VAI 58.4 vs 54.2, Hold 17.0 vs 12.8), while the logo falls from 28.0 to 23.9 and the banner from 14.3 to 8.3. Gaze direction is the likely cause but the designs differ in more than the pose.

strength

Women get to the claim first

Women score higher on the tagline than men in every window and in both designs: VAI +15.6 and +12.1 in the first 3 s, +7.2 and +10.4 in the first 10 s (A and B). In A, men reach the face and pack earlier.

weak evidence

Age groups other than 18–24 are small

18–24 viewers (82 and 83) behave like the overall sample. Groups of 25–34 (28 and 31) and 35+ (7 and 14) are too small to separate real differences from noise.

Conclusions

  • The tagline is the entry point and the pack the anchor: keep both where they are.
  • The brand name is only reliably seen on the pack label. The bottom banner adds little: move the brand name into the tagline-to-pack column, or raise and enlarge the banner.
  • Use design A's profile gaze as the base for brand visibility; test a direct-gaze face with the brand name on the eye line.
  • Women reach the claim sooner than men in both designs: do not move or shrink the tagline without retesting.
  • VAI shows attention, not understanding: confirm the changes with an unaided brand and message recall test.

What to do next

  1. 1

    Move the brand name out of the cold bottom band

    Banner VAI is 14.3 (A) and 8.3 (B). Place the brand name next to the tagline or on the pack at a larger size, or raise and enlarge the banner into the zone the heatmaps show is warm.

    Preserve: The tagline and the pack, which lead the viewing order.

  2. 2

    Use A's profile gaze as the base for brand visibility

    In A the logo and banner score higher in every window (first 3 s: logo VAI 7.9 vs 4.4, banner 3.6 vs 1.2).

  3. 3

    Keep the claim prominent for women

    Women's tagline VAI is 7 to 16 points above men's in every window. Retest before changing the tagline's position or size.

    Preserve: Tagline position and size.

  4. 4

    Test B's face strength without losing the brand

    B holds the face better (VAI 58.4 vs 54.2). Test a direct-gaze face with the brand name on the eye line or beside the face.

The detailed analysis follows: what the scores mean, the viewing order, each design, gender and age. Technical details are in the appendix at the end.

What the scores mean (VAI)

VAI (Visual Attention Index) is RealEye's attention score for an element of the image (the tagline, the pack, the face, the logo). It runs from 0 to 100 and is the average of three simple measures:

Reach

How many viewers looked at it at all. Did people get there?

Speed

How soon they noticed it. How early in the viewing order? It is used here to rank the viewing order.

Hold

How long attention stayed on it. Did people stay?

How to use it

  • Compare, don't grade. VAI is not a percentage of viewers. Use it to rank the elements within a design and to compare the same element across designs, time windows or audiences.
  • Look at the three measures, not just the total. The same VAI can hide very different stories (see the table below).
  • Higher is not always better. A logo can do its job at a moderate score. What matters is that each element scores as the design intends.
  • It shows attention, not outcome. It does not say whether viewers understood, liked or will buy; confirm with a recall or choice test.

Component patterns and what to do

ReachSpeedHoldReadingTypical action
HighHighHighStrong element: almost everyone reaches it, soon, and stays on it.Keep it. Protect its position and size.
HighHighLowSeen fast by most viewers but only glanced at. Normal for a logo; a problem for a claim that must be read.If it must be read, shorten it or give it more room.
HighLowanyReached eventually, but late: it competes with elements ahead of it in the viewing order.Move it earlier in the order or make it more salient.
LowLowLowBlind spot: few viewers reach it, late, and briefly.Relocate, enlarge, raise contrast, or remove clutter around it.
LowanyHighHard to find, but viewers who find it read it: a placement problem, not a content problem.Move it into the path viewers already follow.

What the data says

  • Viewing order in the first 10 s: Tagline (VAI 61.5) → Pack (61.2) → Face (54.2) → Logo (28.0) → Brand banner (14.3). The same order holds in the first 3 and 5 s.
  • The tagline leads from the start: VAI 57.5 in the first 3 s with Reach 80%. The pack catches up: VAI 42.2 → 52.6 → 61.2 and Reach 72% → 83% → 92%.
  • The face builds slowly: VAI 23.6 → 38.3 → 54.2 (Speed 23.7 → 37.0 → 60.4), so it is mostly a second-half element.
  • Logo and banner are the weak spots: Reach 52.8% and 27.1%, Hold 2.7 and 1.2 in the first 10 s. In the first 3 s the banner reaches only 6.6% of viewers.
  • Women lead on the tagline (VAI +15.6 in the first 3 s, +7.2 in the first 10 s versus men); men score higher on the face early (27.8 vs 19.0 in the first 3 s).

What the data says

  • Viewing order in the first 10 s: Tagline → Pack → Face → Logo → Brand banner by VAI Speed (80.3, 74.6, 63.7, 23.6, 7.9). Pack VAI (61.8) edges the tagline (61.7) at 10 s through higher Hold, but the tagline is still noticed first.

Gender and age insights

  • Gender: women score higher on the tagline than men in every window and in both designs (A +15.6, +13.3, +7.2; B +12.1, +10.8, +10.4 VAI points for the first 3, 5 and 10 s), mainly through Speed (+12 to +17). In A, men score higher on the face and pack early (face VAI 27.8 vs 19.0 in the first 3 s).
  • Gender × age: the tagline gap is clearest among 18–24 viewers, where both groups are large enough: women minus men is +14.2 in A (57 vs 24 viewers) and +12.7 in B (44 vs 37) in the first 10 s.
  • Gender: face, pack, logo and banner show no consistent gap between women and men; banner VAI differences are 3 points or less in every window.
  • Age: 18–24 viewers behave like the overall sample. In A, viewers aged 25–34 score higher on the logo (34.2 vs 28.3) and banner (18.9 vs 14.4) in the first 10 s, but with 28 viewers this is a hypothesis, not a finding. In B the 25–34 group scores 12.2 on the banner against 8.5 for 18–24 (31 viewers).
  • Age: viewers aged 35+ (7 in A, 14 in B) and most gender × age cells outside 18–24 are under 30 viewers. Recruit at least 30 viewers per audience if audience-specific recommendations matter.

How to test it next

Design
Randomly assign target viewers to one version each, in a realistic feed or shelf context, with at least 30 Average-or-better viewers per gender and age band.
Primary Outcome
Unaided brand recall and main-message recall in the same respondent, with accepted answers agreed beforehand.
Guardrail
Purchase intent.
Diagnostic Vai Metric
Brand name and logo VAI, Reach and Speed in the first 3 s, by gender and age.

Technical appendix

For analysts and researchers: how the study was run, the data used, and the limits of the evidence.

About this study

Platform
RealEye platform
Eye tracking
Webcam eye tracking: participants viewed the images in their own browsers while RealEye estimated their gaze from their webcams.
Study
#demo Images and Video demo (2023-10-25), stimuli 5 (design A) and 6 (design B) of 15
Participants analysed
Design A: 229 viewers (12 of 241 removed for low data quality). Design B: 227 viewers (5 of 232 removed).
Participant quality filter
Only viewers with data quality Average or better are analysed.
Time windows
First 3 s (0.5–3 s), first 5 s (0.5–5 s) and first 10 s (0.5–10 s), cumulative.
Segments
All viewers; men and women; ages 18–24, 25–34 and 35+; and every gender × age combination. Audiences under 30 viewers are marked †.
Task and exposure
Free viewing, up to 10 s, one image at a time (demo study).
Source
RealEye dashboard: AOI report statistics, AOI VAI report and fixation data, with the filters above.
Tracker precision
Webcam eye tracking is less precise than a lab tracker, so small elements are measured less precisely than large ones.

Viewers with other or unspecified gender, or no recorded age, are in the overall results but not in the gender and age cuts.

Technical notes on VAI

  • Compare like with like: the same element, the same time window and a similar number of viewers (N). Large elements, and elements that overlap others, naturally score higher.
  • Windows are cumulative. "First 3 s" is 0.5–3 s, "first 5 s" is 0.5–5 s and "first 10 s" is 0.5–10 s. The first 0.5 s is skipped to reduce the effect of where viewers happened to be looking when the image appeared. Reach and Speed can only rise as the window grows; Hold is relative to the window, so it can fall even when viewers keep looking.
  • Small groups are noisy. Audiences with fewer than 30 viewers are marked † and should be read as anecdotal.
  • VAI is the equal-weight mean of Reach, Speed and Hold and is not a share of the image's attention.

Evidence and limits

  • No survey or choice data were available, so nothing here shows recall, liking, preference or intent. VAI measures attention only.
  • Webcam eye tracking has less spatial precision than a lab tracker, so small AOIs are measured less precisely than large ones, and AOIs are not directly comparable by size.
  • Only viewers with data quality Average or better are analysed (A: 229 of 241, B: 227 of 232). The embedded dashboard AOI VAI report cannot be quality-filtered and covers all participants with data.
  • Both images sit in the same 15-stimulus study with different viewer counts, so groups probably overlap and order effects are possible; comparisons are indicative.
  • About a third of viewers have other or unspecified gender and about half have no recorded age; they are in the overall results but not in the audience cuts. Audiences under 30 viewers are anecdotal.
  • Heatmaps by audience are drawn from the same fixation data as the dashboard, each scaled to its own maximum; the dashboard's own heatmap is shown for all viewers.
  • Viewing order is a relative hierarchy across viewers (VAI Speed), not an individual scan path. AOI shapes were used as saved on each image and are not identical between the two images.

What would change the recommendation

  • A recall result that favours B.
  • A larger sample showing a reliable age gap.
  • A test with the brand name moved showing no gain in banner or logo VAI.

Definitions

VAI
RealEye's Visual Attention Index (0–100): the equal-weight mean of Reach, Speed and Hold. A relative score, not a share of viewers or of attention.
Reach
Share of viewers who looked at the AOI at least once in the window.
Speed
How soon the AOI is noticed after it becomes visible. Used to rank the viewing order.
Hold
How long attention stays on the AOI relative to the window.
Viewing order
AOIs ranked by VAI Speed: a relative hierarchy across viewers, not one person's scan path.
AOI
Area of Interest: a saved region of the image (tagline, pack, face, logo, brand name).
Windows
First 3, 5 and 10 s are cumulative and start at 0.5 s.
Webcam eye tracking
Gaze estimated from participants' own webcams in the RealEye platform. It shows where attention concentrates, with less precision than lab trackers.
Quality filter
Only viewers with data quality Average or better are analysed.

Sources

  • RealEye dashboard AOI statistics (VAI, Reach, Speed, Hold) per audience and window, data quality Average–Perfect
  • RealEye fixation data for the heatmaps, same filters
  • RealEye AOI VAI report for both designs (all participants with data)
  • No participant-level data included
